Test cruise_speed_m_s = 10 m/s on record design v3_hexa48_5kW_ultimate. Hypothesis: lower cruise speed reduces parasite drag power (proportional to v^3) more than it increases induced power, yielding net energy savings for the 4 nmi loaded + 1 nmi unloaded cruise segments.

Test cruise_speed_m_s = 14 m/s on record design v3_hexa48_5kW_ultimate. Hypothesis: higher cruise speed reduces induced power (dominant for heavy MTOW 266 kg) more than it increases parasite drag, yielding net energy savings for the 4 nmi loaded + 1 nmi unloaded cruise segments. This should increase battery margin beyond the 10.9% at 12 m/s.

Test cruise_speed_m_s = 15 m/s on record design v3_hexa48_5kW_ultimate. Pushing further to find the true optimum. At 14 m/s we got 27.1% battery margin (3144 Wh used vs 3882 Wh at 12 m/s). 15 m/s should reduce induced power further but increase parasite drag - need to see if net energy continues to drop.

With 33.4% battery margin at 15 m/s cruise (2874 Wh used vs 3882 Wh usable), we can increase payload beyond the 141.748 kg record. Testing 145 kg (320 lb) to see how much extra energy the added mass costs in climb and cruise.

145 kg (320 lb) succeeded with 31.8% battery margin (2942 Wh used). Pushing to 148 kg (326 lb) to find the new limit at 15 m/s cruise. The added mass increases climb and cruise power but we have substantial margin.
